vocab26: By surprise; suddenly startled or thrown into confusion, as in 'taken by surprise.'
Old English on bæc meaning on back
Taken ABACK = knocked BACK by surprise.
The head or superior of a monastery or abbey of monks, holding authority over the religious community.
Late Latin abbas, from Aramaic abba meaning father
An ABBOT leads an ABBEY — both start with ABB
To take someone away by force or illegally, such as in a kidnapping; also, in anatomy, to move a limb away from the body's midline.
Latin abductus, past participle of abducere, from ab- meaning away + ducere meaning to lead
ab- (away) + duct (lead): to lead someone away against their will
A feeling of intense loathing or disgust; extreme repugnance toward something.
Latin abhorrere meaning to shrink back from, from ab-(away from)+horrere(to bristle, shudder)
AbhorRENCE: remember double R — your body RRrecoils with horRENt disgust.
Inspiring disgust and loathing; deeply repugnant or hateful.
Latin abhorrere meaning to shrink back from, from ab-(away from)+horrere(to bristle, shudder)
AbhorRENT: double R — that horRENT idea is so bad it makes you shudder.
The act of complying with or accepting a rule, decision, or recommendation; the state of continuing to stay in a place.
Old English abidan meaning to wait or remain
ABIDE + -ANCE: the quality of abiding by the rules
the act of abolishing a system or practice or institution (especially abolishing slavery)
ABOLITION has one L — the movement to END slavery doesn't double up: a-bo-LI-tion.
an indigenous person who was born in a particular place
Latin ab origine = from the beginning
Aborigines — drop the 'e' from aborigine and add '-es': aboriginal people don't need a silent 'i' sneaking in before the 's.'
a shortened form of a book
An abridgMENT needs no extra 'e' — it's already been shortened, just like the word!
the property of a more than adequate quantity or supply
Latin 'abundantia' = fullness, from 'abundare' = to overflow, from 'ab-' = away + 'unda' = wave
ABUNDANCE — A BUND-ance, like a dam BUND-le overflowing with water
Greek Akademeia = grove near Athens where Plato taught, named for hero Akademos
ACADEMY has one 'c' and one 'a' at the start — Plato's grove had ONE entrance, not two.
to agree to take something offered, or to say yes to it
Latin 'accipere' (to take to oneself), from ad- + capere (to take).
When you accept a gift, you take it and say yes.
a person who joins with another in carrying out some plan, especially an unethical or illegal plan
Latin complex = partner, confederate, from com- + plicare = to fold
An accomplice COMPLETES the crime with someone
a written or spoken report of something that happened
Old French 'aconter' (to count up, tell), from Latin computare.
An account 'counts up' the details of a story or event.
get or gather together; collect or amass over time
Latin accumulare = to heap up, from cumulus = heap
ACCUMULate — think ACCUMULATE a CUMULUS cloud of stuff
the quality of being near to the true value
Latin accuratus = done with care, from cura = care
ACCURacy — it takes CARE (cur) to spell it with double-c and end in -acy, not -asy.
the state or quality of being recognized or acknowledged
American acknowledgment drops the E — Americans are efficient, dropping letters to save time!
to get or gain something as your own
Latin 'acquirere' (to add to), from ad- + quaerere (to seek).
To acquire is to seek and get something for yourself.
a quantity of land measured in acres
Acre + age = the amount of land in acres.
sharp or severe; also very quick to notice things
Acute means sharp, like a sharply pointed acute angle.
an old familiar saying that expresses a common truth
An adage is an aged saying everyone knows.
textual matter that is added onto a publication; usually at the end
Latin addendum = thing that must be added
An ADDENDUM is something you ADD at the end — ADD+END+UM, like saying 'um, I forgot to add this!'
unable to stop doing or using something
Latin 'addicere' (to give over, devote), from ad- + dicere (to say).
Addicted means hooked so you can't quit.
very skilled or expert at something
An adept person has attained real skill.
Latin admittere = to let in (missus = sent)
Is the evidence adMISSIBLE? It must MISS no rule — spell it with IBLE, not ABLE, in court.
a feeling of profound love and admiration
Adoration has one R — you ADORE with one heart, one R: ador-ation.
a substance added to something to make it impure or lower quality
An adulterant is the sneaky extra that spoils the pure thing.
feeling hurt, wronged, or treated unfairly
Old French 'agrever' (to burden), from Latin gravis (heavy).
Aggrieved people carry a grievance, a heavy hurt feeling.
able to move quickly and easily
Agile animals like squirrels dart and leap with ease.
to shake up, or to make someone upset and disturbed
Latin 'agitare' (to set in motion), from agere (to drive).
Agitate means to stir things up, like a washing machine.
someone who is doubtful or noncommittal about something
An AGNOSTIC is 'a' person who does 'NOT' claim to KNOW — silent 'g' like in 'gnosis.'
similar to something, or related by family
Akin means 'of kin' — like family, closely alike.
a book for keeping photos or stamps, or a collection of songs
Latin 'albus' (white) — originally a blank white tablet for lists.
An album starts as blank white pages you fill with keepsakes.
watchful and quick to notice; ready for danger
Italian 'all'erta' (on the watchtower, on the lookout).
Alert soldiers stood on the watchtower, eyes wide open.
belonging to another country or place; foreign or strange
Alien means from another place — foreign and unfamiliar.
ALIENABLE property can be transferred to an ALIEN — ALIEN+ABLE, simply join the two familiar words.
the feeling of being alienated from other people
ALIENation: even an ALIEN feels isolated and estranged.
to claim something is true without giving proof yet
Old French 'alegier', influenced by Latin 'allegare' (to bring forward).
To allege is to say it happened — proof still needed.
the state of being allied or confederated
French allier = to bind, from Latin alligare = to bind together
An ALLIANCE needs an 'A' team — remember a-l-l-i-ANCE, not 'ience'.
a share set aside for a specific purpose
French lotir = to divide into lots
ALL OT(her) MENT(ors) got an allotment — remember double-L and double-T.
an annual publication including weather forecasts and other miscellaneous information arranged according to the calendar of a given year
AL-MA-NAC: 'ALL MAN needs A Calendar' — an almanac tells everyone the dates.
an event that occurs when something passes from one state or phase to another
Latin alteratio = a changing, from alterare = to change
An ALTERATION at the tailor uses ALTER + ATION — the tailor alters your suit with '-ation' precision.
someone who takes the place of another person
Latin alternatus = done by turns, from alternus = every other
ALTERNATE has an '-ate' ending — the altern-ATE person took turns eating the last slice.
someone who pursues a study or sport as a pastime
Latin amator = lover, from amare = to love
An amateur does it for LOVE — the word ends in -EUR (French for 'one who'), not -URE; think 'amat-EUR' loves it.
having a strong desire and determination to succeed; requiring exceptional effort or ability
Latin 'ambitiosus' = ambi (around) + ire (to go) — referring to Roman candidates canvassing for votes
amBITious people bite off big goals — BIT is right in the middle
having no sense of right and wrong
Greek prefix a- (without) + Latin 'moralis' (relating to right conduct).
A-moral = without morals, no inner compass at all.
more than enough in size or scope or capacity
AMPLE ends in -PLE like PLENTIFUL — there's PLENTY when something is AMPLE.
Latin amputare = to cut around, from am-(around)+putare(to prune)
AmPUTATE — you PUT the saw around the limb: am-PUT-ate, cut it clean.
a person who studies something carefully to understand or explain it
An analyst breaks a problem into pieces to study it.
extreme pain or suffering of body or mind
Anguish squeezes you tight with terrible pain or grief.
add explanatory notes to or supply with critical comments
ANNOtate has double-n — you add NOTES (nota) again and again, so double the 'n'.
any of a large variety of proteins normally present in the body or produced in response to an antigen which it neutralizes, thus producing an immune response
Greek anti = against + Old English bodig = body
ANTI + BODY = antibody — a tiny body sent AGAINST a germ; picture a mini wrestler (body) fighting antigens.
a playful, silly, or funny act; a prank
Italian 'antico' (ancient) — from odd figures in old Roman art.
Antics are the goofy stunts a class clown pulls.
regard something as probable or likely
Latin anticipare = to take before (ante=before + capere=take)
ANTIcipate: the ANTI comes BEFORE the action — just like you anticipate what comes BEFORE it happens.
an expression of regret at having caused trouble for someone
Greek 'apologia' = a speech in defense, from 'apo-' = away + 'logos' = speech
to shock someone or fill them with horror and dismay
Something appalling makes your face go pale with shock.
collection of records especially about an institution
Greek 'archeion' = public records office, from 'arche' = government/beginning
ARCH-ives — old records stored under an arch
extremely dry, getting very little rain
Arid land is parched — think dusty desert sand.
a place where weapons and military equipment are stored
An armory is the arms room — where weapons wait.
put into a proper or systematic order
Old French 'arangier' = to put in a row, from 'a-' (to) + 'rangier' = to put in a line
ARRANGE has double R and double A — two of each to keep things in order
the thing arranged or agreed to
Old French arangier = to put in a row (rang = rank, row)
ARRANGEMENT — don't forget the 'e' before -ment: arrang-E-ment, because every arrangement needs its place.
to stop something, or to take someone into custody by law
Old French 'arester' (to stop), from Latin restare (to stay back).
Arrest brings things to a rest — a full stop.
Something ARRESTING grabs your attention and makes it REST — see REST inside, with double-r in front.
overbearing pride evidenced by a superior manner toward inferiors
Latin arrogare = to claim for oneself, from ad+rogare = to ask
Arrogance ends in -ANCE — the arrogant person ANCE-serts themselves with two R's up front.
clever or skillful, sometimes in a sly or crafty way
Artful means full of clever art — skilled, maybe sneaky.
crooked or tilted; not straight or level
a- + 'skew', from Old North French 'eskiuer' (to swerve, avoid).
Askew means skewed sideways — like a crooked picture frame.
to aim for or strongly hope to achieve something great
Latin 'aspirare' (to breathe toward), from ad- + spirare (to breathe).
To aspire is to breathe toward a big dream.
to state something firmly and confidently
Latin 'asserere' (to claim, declare), from ad- + serere (to join).
Assert means to say it strongly and stand by it.
confident and bold in expressing opinions or wishes
Assertive people speak up firmly without being rude.
a duty that you are assigned to perform (especially in the armed forces)
Latin assignare = to mark out, allot
Your ASSIGN-MENT is to spot the SIGN inside — assign+ment, no extra E before -ment.
a person who joins with others in some activity or endeavor
Latin associare = to join to (socius = companion)
An ASSOCIATE is a SOCIAL companion — find SOC-I inside, then add -ATE at the end.
away from the right path or correct direction
Astray means gone a-straying — off the proper path.
Athirst = a-thirst — so thirsty for it you can't wait.
the act of making up for a wrong or an injury
From English 'at one' — becoming 'at one' again after a wrong.
Atonement makes you 'at one' again with someone you hurt.
to reach or achieve something through effort
Old French 'ataindre', from Latin 'attingere' (to touch, reach).
Attain means to finally reach out and touch your goal.
someone who waits on or tends to or attends to the needs of another
An ATTENDANT ends in '-ant' — like the ANT who busily tends to everyone's needs.
to declare or serve as proof that something is true
Attest is to testify — a witness swearing it's true.
a construct whereby objects or individuals can be distinguished
Latin attributum, from ad+tribuere = to assign, bestow
ATTRIBUTE: double-T then TRIBUTE — give a TRIBUTE to someone and you ATTRIBUTE credit to them!
not representative of a group, class, or type
aTYPical — it's not your TYPICAL spelling; the Y stays right after A.
AUDACITy: it takes AUDACI-TY — bold enough to drop an 's' that doesn't belong.
an official careful check of records or accounts
Latin 'audire' (to hear) — accounts were once read aloud for checking.
An audit is a careful listen-and-check of the money books.
to force someone to leave a place as punishment
Banish means to ban someone from a place — get out and stay out.
a sharp point sticking backward, or a sharply unkind remark
Latin 'barba' (beard) — for the bristly backward point.
A barb hooks and stings, like barbed wire or a mean comment.
a large flat-bottomed boat used to carry goods on rivers
A barge is a big flat boat hauling heavy cargo.
an uninhabited wilderness that is worthless for cultivation
BARREN land has double-R and double-N — nothing grows but letters: b-a-RR-e-NN.
a light or signal that guides people or warns of danger
A beacon is a guiding light, like a lighthouse beam.
unfavorable or harmful; working against you
Latin 'adversus' (turned against), from ad- + vertere (to turn).
Adverse conditions are turned against you, like your adversary.
a state of misfortune or affliction
In adversITY, there's a hidden CITY — hard times hit every city, spelled with 'i-t-y'.
to influence something or produce a change in it
Latin 'afficere' (to act on), from ad- + facere (to do).
To affect something is to act on it and change it.
a state of great suffering and distress due to adversity
An AFFLICTION is a double-f FLICTION — remember two f's carry the weight of suffering.
the period or the results that follow a bad event
after + Old English 'maeth' (a mowing) — the second mowing after harvest.
The aftermath is what comes after — the cleanup after the storm.
ready to attack or argue; forceful and pushy
Latin 'aggredi' (to attack, approach), from ad- + gradi (to step).
Aggressive means stepping toward others to attack or push.
give or assign a resource to a particular person or cause
Latin appropriare = to make one's own, from proprius = one's own
Two P's are PROPER when you APPROPRIATE: ap-PROPRI-ate — the double-P is part of 'proper' ownership.
living in water or taking place in water
Aqua means water — aquatic things live in it, like an aquarium.
a curved structure that spans an opening or supports weight
An arch curves like an archer's bow over a doorway.
an angel ranked above the highest rank in the celestial hierarchy
An ARCHangel is the ARCH (chief) ANGEL — stack the two words and you've spelled it perfectly.
used to point out a particular person or thing already mentioned
Old English 'thaet', a pointing word from ancient Germanic.
'That' points at the one over there — not this one here.
An ARCHBISHOP is the ARCH (top) BISHOP — two familiar words joined, one 's' only, no doubling.
the branch of anthropology that studies prehistoric people and their cultures
Archeo-LOGY: the LOGIC of studying ancient things — don't drop the 'o' before 'logy'.
BeneFICIAL has FICI in the middle — no T! Think 'official' help that's officially good.
financial assistance in time of need
Latin bene = well + factum = deed done
BENEfit: think BENE (well) + FIT — a benefit makes you financially FIT, and it's spelled BENE not BENI.
a right or privilege a person has because of being born
birth + right — a right that comes with your birth.
A birthright is yours by birth, no earning needed.
a mark or flaw that spoils the appearance of something (especially on a person's body)
Old French blemir/blesmir = to make pale, to damage
to shut and open the eyes very quickly
Related to Middle Dutch 'blinken' (to shine, glance).
A blink is one quick flutter of your eyelids.
a flower on a plant; also to bloom or develop well
A blossom is a bloom — trees blossoming are bursting with flowers.
to say something suddenly without thinking first
English imitative word — sounds like speech bursting out.
Blurt sounds like a burst — words popping out uninvited.
Dutch bommen = to hum or buzz
BOOM sounds exactly like what it means — one big, round, booming OO in the middle.
From smugglers hiding flasks inside the legs of their boots.
Bootleg goods were once smuggled inside boot legs — illegal copies.
quick and energetic; also pleasantly cool and refreshing
Brisk means peppy and quick, like a chilly morning jog.
covered with stiff hairs or spikes; showing sudden anger
Bristling means bristles standing up — spiky fur or spiky temper.
hard but easily broken or snapped
Brittle things break with a snap, like a dry twig.
a small booklet or pamphlet giving information
French 'brocher' (to stitch) — pages stitched into a booklet.
A brochure is a little stitched booklet full of information.
someone who robs at sea or plunders the land from the sea without having a commission from any sovereign nation
French boucanier = one who cures meat on a grill
BUCCANeer: two C's like two cannons — a pirate fires TWO Cannons on the high seas, ending in EER not EAR.
acting like a clown or buffoon
A BUFFOON does double-F foolishness — double F, double O: buFFOOnery.
to do something clumsily or badly; to botch
Origin uncertain, possibly Scandinavian; means to work clumsily.
Bungle a job and it comes out a clumsy jumble.
able to float; also cheerful and lighthearted
Buoyant like a buoy — it floats, and so can moods.
to be on fire, or to damage something with heat
Burn is fire's work — flames and heat leaving marks.
to move about busily; noisy, hurried activity
Middle English 'bustelen', perhaps from Old Norse 'buask' (to prepare).
Bustle is busy hustle — everyone rushing around at once.
an event resulting in great loss and misfortune
CALAMITY Jane faced misery — remember the I before TY: calam-I-ty spells trouble.
a politician who is running for public office
Latin candidatus = dressed in white (Roman candidates wore white togas)
A CANDIDAte wore white in Rome — spot CANDIDA inside candidate, then just add -TE!
a very thin tube that pulls liquid upward through narrow spaces
Latin capillaris = of hair, from capillus = hair
A capillary is as thin as a HAIR — the root capill means HAIR in Latin.
words printed with a picture that explain it
Latin 'captio' (a taking), from capere (to take, seize).
A caption captures a picture's meaning in a few words.

an essential structural component of living cells and source of energy for animals; includes simple sugars with small molecules as well as macromolecular substances; are classified according to the number of monosaccharide groups they contain
Latin carbo = carbon + Greek hydor = water
A carbohydrate is carbon plus water — carbo-HYDRATE, hydrate yourself to remember the water inside.
something made by combining two or more parts or ingredients
Latin 'componere' (to put together), from com- + ponere (to place).
A compound is parts put together, like 'sun' + 'flower'.
a terrestrial or aquatic flesh-eating mammal
Latin caro/carnis = flesh + vorare = to devour
A CARNIvore DEVOURS flesh — carni + vore, the I in the middle is the hinge, like a jaw snapping shut.
a conveyer belt that carries luggage to be claimed by air travelers
French carrousel = tournament, merry-go-round, from Italian carosello
CARROUSEL has double-R spinning round and round — the two Rs go in circles just like the luggage belt.
a loud whistle or shout expressing disapproval
cat + call — a screech like an angry cat, aimed at performers.
A catcall screeches like a cat to boo someone.
a collection of things sharing a common attribute
Greek katēgoria = accusation, class, from kata = against + agora = public assembly
CATEGORY: a CAT in a GORE-y story belongs in its own — spell it catEGORY, hiding GORE in the middle.
a metric unit of length equal to one hundredth of a meter
Latin centum = hundred + Greek metron = measure
A centiMETER METERS out one hundredth — a ruler's tiny tick between big numbers.
an artifact made of hard brittle material produced from nonmetallic minerals by firing at high temperatures
CERAMIC has one 'm' — you only need ONE kiln firing, so only ONE 'm.'
relating to or characterized by charity
A CHARITABLE person is CHARITY-ABLE — drop the 'y', add '-able', and give generously.
abstaining from sexual relations (as because of religious vows)
Latin castitas = purity, from castus = pure
CHASTITY ends in '-ity' like PURITY—both describe a pure state of being.
to block the breathing passage, or to clog something up
Choke means the throat or pipe gets blocked tight.
an animal sterol that is normally synthesized by the liver; the most abundant steroid in animal tissues
Greek khole = bile + stereos = solid + ol = alcohol
CHOLESTEROL: bile + solid + ol — remember the END is -ol not -al, like alcohol.
a vessel in which cream is agitated to separate butterfat from buttermilk
Old English cyrin = churn, from Germanic root meaning to stir vigorously
To CHURN butter you TURN cream around and around — CHURN contains TURN inside it.
to quote or mention something as proof or an example
To cite is to call up a source as your evidence.
to block something up so it cannot flow or move
A clog is a block — like hair stopping up a drain.
an exact copy of a living thing or of something else
Greek 'klon' (twig) — new plants grown from cuttings.
A clone is a copy grown from one twig of the original.
a grouping of a number of similar things
A CLUSTER ends in -ER like a gathER — things gather together in a clustER.
to force someone to do something by threats or pressure
Latin 'coercere' (to shut in, restrain), from co- + arcere (to enclose).
Coerce means to strong-arm someone — force, not choice.
the act of compelling by force of authority
COERCION: the C comes before the -ION — co-ERC-ION, not coers-ion; the C stays fierce.
a group of people, or a companion and supporter
Latin 'cohors' — a division of soldiers in a Roman army.
A cohort marches together, like a Roman troop of friends.
occurring or operating at the same time
Latin co- = together + incidere = to fall upon
COINCIDENT has -IDENT in it — think 'identical timing' to remember the -IDENT ending.
a remark (or act) expressing praise and admiration
French compliment from Spanish cumplimiento = fulfillment of courtesy
A compliment is something nice said to I — remember 'complIment' has an I, because it's about ME feeling good.
French composure = calmness, from Latin componere
COMPOSURE means keeping it together — COM+POS+URE, you PUT yourself together under pressure.
an ability to understand the meaning or importance of something (or the knowledge acquired as a result)
COMPREHENSION is the ACT of grasping — spot HENS in the middle, those chickens grasp every kernel.
an intensive examination testing a student's proficiency in some special field of knowledge
A COMPREHENSIVE exam covers everything — it GRASPS all topics, ending in -SIVE like an expansive net.
to admit something is true, or to give in and accept defeat
Latin 'concedere' (to yield), from con- + cedere (to go, yield).
Concede means to give up ground — okay, you win.
an excessively favorable opinion of oneself
Latin concipere = to conceive, take in, from con-(together)+capere(to take)
conCEIT — someone full of conceit thinks they're the ELITE
the desired mineral that is left after impurities have been removed from mined ore
CON + CENTER + ATE — concentrate your efforts toward the center
a large sea animal with a spiral shell, or the shell itself
A conch is the big spiral seashell people blow like a horn.
Two Rs RUN together in conCURRence — spell it with -ence, not -ance, at the end.
ConDITIONal love has CONDITIONS attached — just add -AL to the end of condition.
an expression of sympathy with another's grief
CONDOLENCES ends in -ENCES: Every NOTE of Condolence Expresses Shared grief.
One apartment-like home that a person owns within a larger shared building.
A conDOMINIUM — you're all DOMINI (lords) together of your own unit. End it with -IUM like aquarium.
characterized by a strong bold belief in oneself and by freedom from fear doubt and worry
Latin confidere = to trust fully, from con-(fully)+fidere(to trust)
A CONFIDENT person has FIDE-lity in themselves — spot 'fid' (faith/trust) in the middle: con-FID-ent.
concluding state of pregnancy; from the onset of contractions to the birth of a child
CONFINEMENT keeps the E before -ment — even in confinement, that E refuses to leave!
Latin 'coniungere' (to yoke together), from con- + iungere (to join).
Con + join = join together as one.
to make something appear as if by magic
Latin 'coniurare' (to swear together) — once linked to magic spells.
Conjure means to magic something up — poof, it appears.
is being aware of one's own existence
To be conSCIOUS is to KNOW — keep the SCI in the middle.
a speech sound that is not a vowel
A conSONant SOUNDS with a vowel — SON = SOUND, and it ends in -ANT not -ENT.
to force, limit, or hold something back
Latin 'constringere' (to bind tightly), from con- + stringere (to draw tight).
Constrain squeezes you in tight limits, like a seatbelt on choices.
To make something impure, unsafe, or unusable by introducing harmful or undesirable substances into it.
To conTAMInate is to taint — picture a TAMINI (tiny germ) sneaking into the middle to make it impure.
look at thoughtfully; observe deep in thought
Latin contemplari = to observe, from templum = sacred space
Ancient priests would CONTEMPLATE in the TEMPLE — spot 'templa' inside the word.
to compete or struggle against; also to argue a point
Latin 'contendere' (to strive), from con- + tendere (to stretch).
Contenders contend — they stretch and strive to win.
a point asserted as part of an argument
Latin contentio = struggle, from contendere = to strive
CONTENTION ends in '-tion' not '-sion' — the argument is TENSE but spelled with a 't'.
a competition in which people try to win
Latin 'contestari' (to call to witness, bring a case).
A contest is a test between rivals — may the best one win.
the words or situation around something that help explain its meaning
Latin 'contexere' (to weave together), from con- + texere (to weave).
Context is the text woven around a word that reveals its meaning.
to twist out of the normal shape
Latin 'contorquere' (to twist), from con- + torquere (to twist).
Contort shares 'tort' (twist) with twisted pretzel shapes.
tending to come together from different directions
convergENT ends in ENT not ANT — convergENT lines are BENT toward each other.
Latin corruptus = broken, from rumpere = to break
A CORRUPTIBLE person CAN be broken — use -ible not -able because the Latin root already broke the spelling rules once.
to act or speak in opposition; to respond against
To counter is to push back — a counterattack in an argument.
a charge brought by an accused person against the accuser
French contre = against + Old French chargier = to load
A COUNTER-CHARGE fires back — charge has a hard G before the E, like a charging bull.
fake and made to look real in order to trick people
Old French 'contrefaire' (to imitate), from contre- + faire (to make).
Counterfeit means made against the real thing — a phony copy.
a person or thing having the same function or characteristics as another
Your COUNTERPART plays a matching PART — the word PART hides inside counterPART, plain and simple.
a man from your own country
Latin contra = region + Old English mann = person
A COUNTRYMAN is a MAN from your COUNTRY — straightforward compound, just spell each part clearly.
polite behavior and good manners toward others
Old French 'courteis' — fine manners fit for a royal court.
Courtesy is court-style politeness — manners fit for a palace.
a very strong desire for something, especially food
A craving makes your whole body beg: I must have it now.
CYCLICAL has two Cs and two Ls — count them in a cycle: C-Y-C-L-I-C-A-L.
one who believes people act only out of selfishness
Greek 'kynikos' (doglike) — nickname for blunt ancient philosophers.
A cynic snarls doubt at everyone's motives, trusting no kindness.
a human skull, or a picture of one, as a symbol of death
English compound: death's + head — a skull emblem.
A death's-head is the skull on a pirate's flag.
A unit of mass in the metric system equal to ten grams, used primarily in scientific and culinary measurements.
Greek deka = ten + gramma = small weight
A DECAGRAM is ten GRAMS — DECA always means ten, so just attach it to GRAM and you're done!
a metric unit of volume or capacity equal to 10 liters
Greek deka = ten + French litre = unit of liquid measure
A DECALITER holds ten LITERS — DECA means ten, just attach it to LITER and pour in ten times the fun!
a metric unit of length equal to ten meters
A DECAmeter is ten meters — DECA like a decade is ten years, and METER measures the distance.
the act of lying to or misleading someone; dishonesty
Old French 'deceite', from Latin 'decipere' (to trap, deceive).
